dimension_grades.evidence: The Redis connection pool false lead is described in extensive detail — reading ioredis source code, finding a closed GitHub issue, writing a test harness — spanning a full section of the post.

The author explicitly owns their mistakes: "I'd spent a day and a half reading library source code for a problem I hadn't even profiled yet" and "the real bug — the one that cost us three and a half extra days — was me."
"By Tuesday afternoon — a full day and a half in" and "The whole thing took four days. It should have taken four hours" make the wasted time explicit and painful.

The tone is wry and self-aware — e.g., "I'd been doing the engineering equivalent of diagnosing a car engine by reading the owner's manual in a different room from the car" — without veering into self-pity.
The author shows the confusing heap snapshot evidence — plain JS objects, not Redis-shaped — and the puzzlement: "No caching layer. No in-memory store. At least, not one I remembered writing."
Clues build incrementally: sawtooth pattern → Redis theory debunked → heap snapshots showing plain objects → retainer chain → grep of node_modules → the offending Map in the validation library.

The root cause (the unbounded cache Map in the validation library) doesn't appear until after multiple sections of wrong turns, confusion, and narrowing, landing as a payoff in 'The Clue I Walked Past Twice.'

Emotional states are woven throughout: the dopamine hit of a false lead ("I felt that little dopamine hit of I've found it"), genuine confusion ("I was genuinely confused"), and nervous relief ("refreshing the dashboard like a nervous parent checking a baby monitor").

Each takeaway names a specific behavior: "I now take a heap snapshot before forming any theory" (a sequencing rule added to a runbook), "I search node_modules early," and "before I spend more than two hours on a hypothesis, I explain it to someone."
"I'm not going to tell you to 'always monitor your memory' or 'profile before optimizing.' You know that. I knew that. I did it anyway."

Each takeaway connects to a specific narrative moment: the heap snapshot rule ties to the wasted day on Redis, the node_modules search ties to missing the validation library, and the say-it-out-loud rule ties to Priya's question at standup.
The framing treats the reader as a peer: "You know that. I knew that" and "Skipping the Stuff You Already Know" explicitly position the reader as someone who doesn't need basic advice.
There are only two code snippets in the entire post — the offending validation library code and the before/after fix — each earning its place in the narrative.
Critical lines are annotated with inline comments: "// <-- THIS LINE" on the cache key line, "// cache grows forever, never evicted" on the set call, and "// disable internal cache" on the fix.
The second snippet explicitly shows before ("default caching behavior (unbounded Map)") and after ("caching disabled, we handle performance ourselves") with labeled comments.

Before the first snippet, the prose explains what to look for: "I opened the relevant file and found this" after establishing the retainer chain context; before the second, "the library accepted a configuration option I'd never noticed."

Key scenes include concrete details: "4:47 PM on a Friday," "PagerDuty notification lit up my phone," "refreshing the dashboard like a nervous parent checking a baby monitor," and specific metrics like "RSS was sitting at 1.2 GB."
Real tool names are used throughout: PagerDuty, Datadog, Chrome DevTools, Kafka, Postgres, Kubernetes, Jira, ioredis, ajv, Slack.

Important moments are dramatized as scenes with action: "I was halfway through writing a Jira ticket... when the PagerDuty notification lit up my phone" and "Priya finally asked in standup what I'd found, and when I described my Redis theory out loud, I heard how thin it sounded."
